section_summary: This section continues a historical study of Japan, moving from Tokugawa intellectual life and the opening of the country through the Meiji Restoration, constitutional government, industrialization, and the Sino-Japanese War. It then traces Japanese expansion in Korea, Manchuria, Siberia, Shandong, and North China through the creation of Manchukuo and Japan’s withdrawal from the League of Nations. The closing pages examine the economic “life-line” argument for Manchuria and an official ideological defense of Japanese leadership and expansion in Asia.

subfiles.title: Study of Japanese history, modernization, and expansionism, Chapters 4–6 (continuation)
subfiles.doc_type: historical study or instructional book excerpt
subfiles.about: A historical and political analysis of Japan’s transformation from Tokugawa society into a modern industrial and imperial power.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt begins by discussing Tokugawa intellectual life, nationalism, Dutch learning, and the pressures that preceded Commodore Perry’s opening of Japan. It examines the Meiji Restoration, abolition of feudalism, creation of a centralized bureaucracy and constitution, development of mass education, a conscript army, transportation, and state-assisted industry. It then traces Japanese expansion from the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars through the annexation of Korea, intervention in Siberia, seizure of Manchuria, establishment of Manchukuo, and conflict with the League of Nations. The final pages question Manchukuo’s value as Japan’s economic “life-line” and present an official rationale for Japanese expansion and leadership in Asia.
